nameStory: The Common True Katydid is literally the original "katydid" — its distinctive three-part call sounds exactly like "ka-ty-did" when the males sing on summer evenings. This rasping, rhythmic song was so memorable to early settlers that they named the entire katydid family after this one species' musical proclamation.
description: The Common True Katydid is a chunky, leaf-green insect that looks like a walking leaf with attitude. These robust insects can grow up to 2 inches long, with powerful hind legs and leaf-like wing covers that help them blend into deciduous tree canopies. Unlike their grasshopper cousins, katydids are surprisingly clumsy fliers and prefer to walk, run, or hop through the branches where they munch on leaves.

idTips.label: Three-part call
idTips.description: Listen for the unmistakable "ka-ty-DID" song on summer nights — a loud, rasping three-pulse rhythm that sounds scratchy and mechanical, like someone rapidly dragging a comb across cardboard

idTips.label: Leaf-like wings
idTips.description: Wing covers are bright green and textured like rough leaves, with visible veining that mimics real foliage — run your finger along them and they feel papery and slightly bumpy

idTips.label: Chunky build
idTips.description: Much more robust and thick-bodied than other katydids, with a stocky appearance that makes them look almost clumsy compared to their more delicate relatives

idTips.label: Ground movement
idTips.description: Watch for their distinctive walking and hopping behavior rather than flying — they move through branches like tiny green bulldozers rather than graceful leapers

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Noticeably large for a katydid at up to 2 inches long, making them one of the biggest green insects you'll encounter in New England trees

habitat: Common True Katydids live high in the canopy of deciduous forests throughout New England, particularly favoring oak, maple, and hickory trees. You'll find them from sea level to moderate elevations, especially in mature woodlands where the tree crowns form a continuous canopy. They rarely venture down from the treetops, preferring to stay 20-40 feet up where the best leaves grow.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active, but you might find overwintering eggs tucked into bark crevices of deciduous trees.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season when adults are calling loudly from treetops — listen for their signature "ka-ty-did" songs starting in July and continuing through August.
seasonality.fall: Calling continues into early fall, though it becomes less frequent as temperatures drop and adults begin to die off after mating season.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died, leaving only eggs to survive the cold months embedded in tree bark until next year's hatch.

funFact: The Common True Katydid is so bad at flying that it has essentially given up trying — instead of soaring between trees like other insects, these chunky characters prefer to walk everywhere, earning them the nickname "the pedestrians of the treetops."
confusionNotes: Other katydid species make clicking, buzzing, or continuous trilling sounds, but only the Common True Katydid makes that classic three-part "ka-ty-DID" call. Remember: if it doesn't say "katydid," it's probably not the true katydid!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the "true" katydid, this species is actually just one of many katydid types — the "true" part comes from being the original species that gave katydids their name, making it the most "authentic" katydid rather than the only real one.
compareHints: Since Common True Katydids are the only Pterophylla species in New England, compare them to other local katydids like the Broad-winged Katydid, which has a more continuous buzzing call rather than the distinct three-part rhythm. Common True Katydids are also much chunkier and less graceful than most other katydid species, with their distinctive preference for walking over jumping.
